processing: Medicinal herbs are decocted in water, classically simmered in a clay pot. Formulas differ from shop to shop, and many are now also sold as sachets or canned drinks.
harvest_season: Not applicable: a category of herbal decoctions made from many plants, drunk all year and especially in hot weather.
appearance_dry: Mixed dried roots, stems, leaves and flowers, depending on the formula.
appearance_liquor: Most shop liangcha is nearly black and opaque to dark brown; flower-based kinds are much lighter.
appearance_wet: Dark, softened herbs, usually strained out before serving.
taste_profile: Usually bitter with some sweetness behind it, medicinal and earthy; lighter kinds are floral or sweet.

brewing.notes: The Guangdong home method: bring to the boil in a clay pot, simmer on low for about 30 minutes, then rest 15 minutes with the lid on. Drink before it has gone fully cold.

vintage_note: Not sold by year. It comes freshly boiled by the bowl in liangcha shops, as dated herb packs and sachets, and as canned or boxed drinks with a best-before date. Drink shop tea the same day.
description:
Liangcha is not one tea but a whole family of Cantonese herbal drinks, made from medicinal plants and meant in Chinese medicine to clear heat and damp. It is at home in Guangdong, Hong Kong and Macau, and it is popular in Chinese communities in Malaysia and Singapore. The name means cool tea, yet it is often served warm and usually contains no tea leaf.

Each shop guards its own formula, and many have passed theirs down the family. Well-known kinds include 24 Flavors, Five Flower Tea, Xia Sang Ju, and sugarcane with cogon root.

First-timers are often surprised: most of it is almost black and bitter with a sweetish end. Some shops serve small sweet snacks to help it down, and milder flower or fruit kinds are a kinder place to start.

Today you can get it at a shop counter, in sachets or in a supermarket can. The ingredients matter more than the label: some herbs are strongly cooling, and some have raised safety questions. Prunella has shown immune and liver effects in animal tests, so do not treat liangcha as harmless by default, particularly in long or heavy use, in pregnancy, or alongside medicines.
history:
The origin of liangcha is not clearly recorded. A popular story credits the Eastern Jin physician Ge Hong, who came to the far south and studied fever illnesses there, but that remains tradition rather than documented fact.

Shops became an institution in Guangzhou, Hong Kong and Macau, some running for well over a century. Wong Lo Kat is the most famous name. Packaged drinks and sachets arrived later and carried liangcha into convenience stores.

After a joint effort by Guangdong, Hong Kong and Macau begun in 2006, liangcha preparation was entered on China's national list of intangible cultural heritage. In 2006 Chinese health authorities also named 52 plants as possible promoters of cancer in Guangdong; the local food industry replied that liangcha does not use them.
